SQLite is awesome. But even for local desktop apps there are edge cases where PostgreSQL is demonstrably better or faster. If you're going to build a Unix distro & desktop environment from scratch, whether you base it on top of SQLite or PostgreSQL is one of the most important decisions you'll need to make.

I'm still formulating my "Howard Roark of Software" philosophy, and I think I'd like to focus on stand-alone desktop apps rather than give in to the temptation of making everything browser-based and client-server, #zomgHTML6. I want to encourage people to run their software locally, or at least on their seastead's local app server, with petabytes of local content making dependence on outside Internet less relevant.

For example, instead of YouTube you can have a blockchain-based database of all videos on P2P networks (IPFS, BitTorrent, etc), with everyone having the complete metadata on all videos - why not, when the cost per terabyte will continue to fall. You can then run your own full-text search and recommendation algorithms without Google commies getting in the way. SQLite has most of the needed features, but it starts to fall behind PostgreSQL more and more at this scale. PG has hundreds of great extensions.

And you probably still need some client-server mechanisms - such a multi-terabyte monster app might fit on a high-end laptop, but not a waterproof tablet from which you might want to watch videos... So you quickly realize that with technologies like SQLite-based local apps you end up reinventing the wheel...

Plus of course there's the fact that not everything is comparable to a desktop app. Every corporation has huge databases, and most of them are still married to Oracle, which is crippled by design and has 5+ figure license costs, which is insane! PostgreSQL is our best tool for liberating the business world.
